inline.s: The five dharmas are real, and so too are the three self-natures;
The practitioner who contemplates thus does not depart from Suchness.
Depending on the marks of dependent arising, one falsely imagines all kinds of names;
Those marks of false imagining all exist because of dependent arising.
With wisdom one observes well: no objects, and no false imagining;
In the real there is nothing at all—how could discrimination arise?
If the perfected nature existed, it would be apart from being and non-being;
Since it is already apart from being and non-being, how could there be two natures?
False imagining holds to two natures, but the two natures are mere postulates;
Discrimination sees all kinds of things—this is the pure ones’ own domain.
One falsely imagines all kinds of marks and discriminates within dependent arising;
Whoever holds a discrimination other than this falls into the theories of the sectarians.
Because of all false views, one falsely imagines false imagining;
One who is free of these two imaginings—for him there is the real Dharma.”

Mahāmati the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, be pleased to tell us of the marks of the noble wisdom realized by oneself, and of the marks of the One Vehicle. Then I and the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, having gained this skill in means, will not awaken to the Buddha-Dharma through the help of another.”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, relying on the noble teachings, is without discrimination; dwelling alone in quiet seclusion, he observes his own awareness and awakens not through another; free of the views of discrimination, he rises higher and higher and enters the Tathāgata’s ground. Such practice is called the marks of the noble wisdom realized by oneself. What are the marks of the One Vehicle? It is the realization and knowledge of the path of the One Vehicle. And what is it to know the path of the One Vehicle? It is to be free from the discriminations of grasping and grasped, and to dwell just as it is. Mahāmati, this path of the One Vehicle is the Tathāgata’s alone; it cannot be attained by the sectarians, the two vehicles, Brahmā the Heaven-King, or others.”
Mahāmati said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, why do you speak of three vehicles and not of the One Vehicle?”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, it is because the hearers and the solitary realizers have no Dharma of their own for final nirvāṇa that I speak of the One Vehicle. They rely solely on the Tathāgata’s teaching of taming and detachment, and by such practice attain liberation—it is not their own attainment. Moreover, they have not yet destroyed the obstruction of knowledge and the habitual energies of karma, they have not realized the non-self of dharmas, and they are not yet said to have passed beyond the inconceivable transformation-death. Therefore I speak of three vehicles. But if they can put an end to all the habits of fault and realize the non-self of dharmas, then, having risen from the intoxication of samādhi and awakened within the undefiled realm, they cultivate all merits in the world-transcending, supreme, undefiled realm, fulfill them all, and attain the inconceivable, sovereign Dharma-body.” Then the World-Honored One repeated these verses:
“The vehicle of the gods, the vehicle of Brahmā, the vehicles of the hearers and solitary realizers,
And the vehicle of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas—all these vehicles are spoken by me.
As long as a mind arises, no vehicle is final;
But when that mind is turned and extinguished, there is no vehicle and no rider.
Since no vehicle is established, I speak of the One Vehicle;
To gather in the foolish, I speak of distinctions among the vehicles.
Liberation is of three kinds: freedom from all afflictions,
And the non-self of dharmas, and the equal wisdom’s liberation.
Like a log in the sea, ever turning with the waves;
So too is the hearer’s mind, tossed about by the wind of marks.
Though he has put an end to arisen afflictions, he is still bound by habitual energies;
Drunk on the wine of samādhi, he dwells in the undefiled realm.
That is no final destination, yet he falls back no more;
Having gained the body of samādhi, he knows not even the passing of a kalpa.
Like a man drunk and unconscious, who awakens only when the wine has worn off;
So too is the hearer: after awakening, he shall become a Buddha.”
At that time the Buddha said to Mahāmati the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva: “Now I shall tell you of the marks of the distinctions of the mind-made body. Listen well, listen well, and ponder it rightly.”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, the mind-made body is of three kinds. What are the three? They are: the mind-made body accomplished by entering samādhi, the mind-made body that awakens to the self-nature of dharmas, and the mind-made body of the class-born that acts without effort. Practitioners attain them gradually after entering the first ground. Mahāmati, what is the mind-made body accomplished by entering samādhi? It is this: on the third, fourth, and fifth grounds one enters samādhi, is apart from all kinds of mind, still and unmoving; the ocean of mind no longer stirs the waves of the turning consciousnesses, and one understands that the appearances of the mind’s objects are all nothing at all. This is called the mind-made body accomplished by entering samādhi. What is the mind-made body that awakens to the self-nature of dharmas? It is this: on the eighth ground one understands that dharmas are like illusions, all without marks; the mind turns from its dependence and dwells in the illusion-like samādhi and other samādhis, able to manifest immeasurable sovereign spiritual powers, blooming like a flower, quick and according to one’s wish, like an illusion, a dream, a shadow, an image—not made of the four elements, yet resembling what is made; complete in all bodily marks and adorned, entering all Buddha-lands and understanding the nature of all dharmas. This is called the mind-made body that awakens to the self-nature of dharmas. What is the mind-made body of the class-born that acts without effort? It is this: to understand and penetrate the marks of the Dharma realized by all Buddhas themselves. This is called the mind-made body of the class-born that acts without effort. Mahāmati, these three kinds of bodily marks should be diligently observed.”
“My Mahāyāna is no vehicle, nor sound, nor letter;
Not truth, not liberation, nor is it the end of marklessness.
Yet riding the Mahāyāna, sovereign in samādhi,
One has all kinds of mind-made bodies, adorned with sovereign flowers.”

At that time Mahāmati the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has spoken of the five uninterrupted offenses—what are the five? Whoever commits them falls into the Avīci Hell.”

The Buddha said to Mahāmati: “The five uninterrupted offenses are these: killing the mother, killing the father, killing an arhat, breaking the harmonious Saṅgha, and, with an evil and rebellious mind, drawing the Buddha’s blood. Mahāmati, what is the mother of beings? Craving, which draws forth love and rejoices together with greed, nurturing as a mother does. What is the father? Ignorance, which causes birth in the settlements of the six sense-fields. Cutting off these two roots is called killing the father and mother. What is killing an arhat? It is this: the dormant afflictions are an enemy, breaking out like poison in a rat; to cut them off utterly is therefore called killing an arhat. What is breaking the harmonious Saṅgha? It is this: the aggregates, whose marks differ, are gathered together in combination; to cut them off utterly is called breaking the Saṅgha. What is drawing the Buddha’s blood with an evil mind? It is this: the body of the eight consciousnesses falsely gives rise to thought and perception, and one sees self-marks and common marks outside one’s own mind; with the undefiled evil mind of the three liberations one cuts off utterly that Buddha of the body of the eight consciousnesses. This is called drawing the Buddha’s blood with an evil mind. Mahāmati, these are the inner five uninterrupted offenses; whoever commits them immediately realizes and bears witness to the true Dharma.

“Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall now tell you of the outer five uninterrupted offenses, so that you and the other Bodhisattvas, having heard this meaning, may give rise to no doubt in future ages. What are the outer five uninterrupted offenses? They are the uninterrupted offenses spoken of in other teachings. If anyone commits them, he cannot realize the three liberations in this very life. Only the Tathāgata, the great Bodhisattvas, and the great hearers, seeing someone committing the actions of uninterrupted offense, wishing to urge him on and make him mend his ways, display by spiritual power the doing of the same deeds; he repents at once, eradicates them, and realizes liberation—all of which is a transformation, not a real doing. If one truly commits the actions of uninterrupted offense, he will never realize liberation in this present body. The exception is one who awakens to understand that what his own mind displays is the support and dwelling of his own body, and is free of the view of grasping self and mine; or one who, in a later life, is born elsewhere, meets a good friend, is free of the fault of discrimination, and only then realizes liberation.”
“Craving is called the mother, ignorance is the father;
Consciousness that knows the objects—this is called the Buddha.
The dormant afflictions are the arhat, the gathered aggregates the Saṅgha;
To cut them off without remainder—this is called the uninterrupted deed.”
At that time Mahāmati the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, be pleased to tell me of the essential nature of all the Buddhas.”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, to awaken to the two kinds of non-self, to remove the two obstructions, to be free of the two kinds of death, and to cut off the two afflictions—this is the essential nature of the Buddha. Mahāmati, when the hearers and solitary realizers attain this Dharma, they too are called Buddhas; for this reason I speak only of the One Vehicle.”
“Knowing well the two non-selves, removing the two obstructions and two afflictions,
And the inconceivable death—therefore is one named Tathāgata.”

At that time Mahāmati the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, with what secret intent did the Tathāgata proclaim before the great assembly: ‘I am all the Buddhas of the past’? And he told of hundreds of thousands of birth-stories: ‘At that time I was King Mūrdhaja, the great elephant, the parrot, Moonlight, Wondrous Eyes, and so forth.’”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Fully Awakened, relying on the secret intent of the four kinds of equality, speaks thus before the great assembly: ‘In former times I was the Buddha Krakucchanda, the Buddha Kanakamuni, and the Buddha Kāśyapa.’ What are the four? They are: equality of words, equality of speech, equality of body, and equality of Dharma. What is equality of words? It is this: I am named Buddha, and all Tathāgatas are also named Buddha; the name Buddha is without difference—this is called equality of words. What is equality of speech? It is this: I utter speech in sixty-four kinds of Brahmā voice, and all Tathāgatas utter this same speech; the kalaviṅka bird’s Brahmā-voiced nature, neither increasing nor decreasing, without any difference—this is called equality of speech. What is equality of body? It is this: I and all Buddhas are equal without difference in the Dharma-body, its bodily marks, and its minor marks, except that to tame all kinds of beings we manifest bodies of the same class as they—this is called equality of body. What is equality of Dharma? It is this: I and all Buddhas alike realize the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—this is called equality of Dharma. Therefore the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Fully Awakened, speaks thus before the great assembly.”
“Kāśyapa and Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni—these are I;
Relying on the four equalities, I speak thus to the Buddha’s sons.”

At that time Mahāmati the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has said: ‘On a certain night I attained the highest perfect enlightenment, and on a certain night I shall enter nirvāṇa; in the interval I have not spoken a single word, nor have I already spoken, nor shall I yet speak—what is spoken is not the Buddha’s speaking.’ With what secret intent did the World-Honored One speak these words?”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, it is relying on two secret dharmas that I speak thus. What are the two dharmas? They are: the Dharma realized by oneself, and the Dharma that primordially abides. What is the Dharma realized by oneself? It is this: what all Buddhas have realized I also realize, neither increasing nor decreasing; it is the domain of realized wisdom, apart from the marks of words, apart from the marks of discrimination, apart from the marks of names. What is the Dharma that primordially abides? It is this: the original nature of dharmas, like gold within the ore; whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, the Dharma abides and the Dharma’s station stands, and the Dharma-realm and Dharma-nature are all forever abiding. Mahāmati, it is like a man walking in a wide wilderness who sees an ancient road, level and old, leading to an ancient city; he follows it and enters, and there rests and plays. Mahāmati, what do you think? Did that man make this road and all the things in the city?”
He replied: “No, indeed.”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, the Suchness realized by me and all Buddhas, and the ever-abiding Dharma-nature, are likewise so. Therefore it is said: from the attainment of Buddhahood to nirvāṇa, in the interval I have not spoken a single word, nor have I already spoken, nor shall I yet speak.”
“On a certain night attaining perfect enlightenment, on a certain night passing into nirvāṇa;
In the interval between these two, I have spoken nothing at all.
The Dharma realized by oneself, the primordially abiding Dharma—therefore do I speak this secret word;
I and all Tathāgatas are not the least bit different.”

At that time Mahāmati the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, be pleased to tell us of the marks of existence and non-existence of all dharmas. Then I and the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, free of these marks, will quickly attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, beings in the world mostly fall into two views, namely the view of existence and the view of non-existence. Falling into the two views, they do not think of the supramundane. What is the view of existence? It is this: that dharmas truly arise from causes and conditions, and are not unreal; that real dharmas are born from causes and conditions, and are not born without dharmas. Mahāmati, one who speaks thus speaks of no cause. What is the view of non-existence? It is this: knowing that feeling, greed, hatred, and delusion exist, yet falsely supposing and saying that they do not. Mahāmati, there are also those who discriminate marks of existence but do not accept that dharmas exist, and those who know that the Tathāgata, the hearers, and the solitary realizers are without the nature of greed, hatred, and delusion, yet suppose them to be non-existent. Among these, who is the destroyer?”
Mahāmati replied: “One who holds that the nature of greed, hatred, and delusion exists and afterwards takes it as non-existent is called a destroyer.”

The Buddha said: “Excellent! You understand my question. This person is not only a destroyer in that he denies greed, hatred, and delusion; he also destroys the Tathāgata, the hearers, and the solitary realizers. Why? Because afflictions are unobtainable within or without, and their essential nature is neither different nor not different. Mahāmati, the nature of greed, hatred, and delusion is unobtainable whether within or without, because it has no essential nature and nothing can be grasped; the hearers, the solitary realizers, and the Tathāgata are by nature liberated, for there is nothing that binds and no cause of binding. Mahāmati, if there were a binder and a cause of binding, there would be something bound; to speak thus is to be called a destroyer—this is to be without marks. Relying on this meaning I speak in secret intent: better to raise the view of a self as great as Mount Sumeru than to raise the view of emptiness with overweening pride. One who raises this view is called a destroyer, falls into the self-marks and common marks of longing and desire, and does not understand that all dharmas are manifested by mind alone. Because he does not understand, he sees outer dharmas as momentary and impermanent, evolving and differing, the marks of aggregates, elements, and sense-fields continuing and flowing on, arising and again ceasing—false discrimination, apart from the marks of letters—and so he too becomes a destroyer.”
“Existence and non-existence are the two extremes, and so too is all that the mind ranges over;
Purify yourself of all their ranging, and the equal mind is stilled.
Do not grasp at objects, yet do not annihilate into nothingness;
There is a wondrous real Suchness, the domain of all the noble ones.
What primordially was not, yet comes to be; having come to be, it ceases again;
Existence and non-existence through causes—these do not abide in my Dharma.
Not sectarian, not Buddha, not self, not other beings;
What is produced by conditions—how can it be got as non-existent?
Whoever holds that it is produced by conditions, and then again says it is non-existent;
Evil views speak of it as arising, and false imagining conceives being and non-being.
If one knows that nothing is born, then nothing ceases either;
Seeing the world as wholly empty and still, one is free of both being and non-being.”

At that time Mahāmati the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again requested the Buddha: “World-Honored One, be pleased to tell us of the marks of the goal and the teaching. Then I and the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, understanding this meaning well, will not follow the false understandings of all the many, and will quickly attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, all the two vehicles and all Bodhisattvas have two kinds of marks of the dharma of the goal. What are the two? They are: the marks of the dharma of the goal, and the marks of the dharma of verbal teaching. The marks of the dharma of the goal are this: one’s own realization of a surpassing mark, apart from the discriminations of letters and words, entering the undefiled realm and accomplishing the practices of one’s own ground, passing beyond all incorrect thought and perception, taming Māra and the sectarians, and giving rise to the light of wisdom—this is called the marks of the dharma of the goal. The marks of the dharma of verbal teaching are this: to teach the nine divisions of all kinds of teachings, apart from the marks of oneness and difference, being and non-being, and by skillful means to lead beings’ minds according to their kind into this Dharma—this is called the marks of the dharma of verbal teaching. You and all the Bodhisattvas should diligently learn and practice them.”
“Goal and verbal teaching, self-realization and the teachings;
If one can know and see them well, one follows not the false understandings of others.
As the foolish discriminate it, it is not the true mark;
Would they not seek deliverance? Yet nothing can be got.
Observing all conditioned things, birth and ceasing and the like continue on;
One increases the two views, inverted and knowing nothing.
Nirvāṇa is apart from mind and mental factors; this one Dharma alone is real;
Seeing the world as wholly false, like an illusion, a dream, a plantain tree.
There is no greed, no hatred, no delusion, and no person either;
From craving the aggregates are born, as things seen in a dream.”

At that time Mahāmati the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, be pleased to tell me of the marks of false discrimination. How does this false discrimination arise? From what does it arise? Because of what does it arise? From whom is it born? Why is it called false discrimination?”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, excellent, excellent! Out of compassion for the gods and humans of the world you ask this meaning, which brings great benefit and great peace. Listen well, listen well, and ponder it rightly; I shall tell you.”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, all beings, in the face of all kinds of objects, cannot understand what their own minds display; they suppose grasping and grasped, and cling falsely, giving rise to all discriminations and falling into the views of being and non-being. They increase the habitual energies of the sectarians’ false views. When mind and mental factors arise in correspondence, they cling to outer meanings as all kinds of obtainable things, and fix their attachment on self and what belongs to self. Therefore it is called false discrimination.”

Mahāmati said: “If it is so, then the nature of all outer meanings is apart from being and non-being, yet marks of views arise. World-Honored One, the supreme truth is likewise so: apart from all measures of the senses, apart from thesis, reason, and analogy. World-Honored One, why is it that concerning all kinds of meanings you say discrimination arises, while in the supreme truth you do not say it arises? Is the World-Honored One’s word not contrary to reason, since in one place you say it arises and in another you do not? World-Honored One, you also say that false discrimination falls into the view of being and non-being. But just as illusions are all kinds of unreal things, so too is discrimination: it is apart from the marks of being and non-being. Why then do you say it falls into the two views? Does this statement not fall into a worldly view?”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, discrimination is neither born nor ceases. Why? Because the marks of discriminating being and non-being do not arise; because all outer dharmas that are seen are nothing at all; because one understands that they are only what one’s own mind displays. It is only because foolish people discriminate all kinds of dharmas of their own minds and cling to all kinds of marks that I speak thus. So that they may know that all they see is their own mind, cut off all the views and clingings of self and what belongs to self, be free of the evil causes and conditions of doing and done, and, awakening to mind-only, turn their mental delight; so that they may clearly understand the grounds and enter the Buddha’s realm, and abandon the discriminating views of the five dharmas and the self-natures. Therefore I say: false discrimination clings to the arising of all kinds of objects displayed by one’s own mind; when this is understood as it really is, one attains liberation.”
“From causes and from conditions, the world is born;
Corresponding to the four propositions, not knowing my Dharma,
The world is not born from being or non-being, nor from both or neither.
Why do foolish people discriminate dependent arising?
Not existent and not non-existent, nor again both and neither;
Seeing the world thus, the mind turns and realizes non-self.
No dharma is born, because it is born from conditions;
What conditions have made—what is made is not born.
A fruit does not give birth to itself, for two fruits would be the fault;
Since there are no two fruits, no existing nature can be got.
Observing all conditioned dharmas, apart from the grasper and the grasped;
One decides that they are only mind; therefore I speak of the measure of mind.
In the self-nature’s own place of measure, objects and dharmas are both abandoned;
The ultimate, wondrous, pure matter—I call it the measure of mind.
A self is posited as a mere name, yet in truth it cannot be got;
The aggregates are names for aggregates, and all have no real thing.
There are four kinds of equality: mark, cause, and what is born;
Non-self is the fourth—this the practitioner observes.
Apart from all views, and from the discriminations of grasper and grasped;
Without attainment and without birth—this I call the measure of mind.
Not existent and not non-existent, free of both being and non-being;
Thus is mind also free—this I call the measure of mind.
Suchness, emptiness, the ultimate, nirvāṇa, and the Dharma-realm;
